opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a common misconception that what you need is some kind of exotic, deeply specialized skill set. In my experience, the thing that matters most is being a really solid, pragmatic research engineer. That's a bit different from being a great software engineer in the traditional sense.

A lot of traditional software engineering is about building robust, maintainable systems that will last for years. A lot of research engineering is about getting an experiment running as quickly as possible, finding out whether your idea is any good, and then throwing most of the code away. So the most valuable skill is often fast iteration: going from "I have a hypothesis" to "I have a plot that tells me something" in hours rather than weeks.

Within that, a few things stand out to me.

**Debugging and skepticism.** In ML, bugs often don't crash your code. They just quietly give you wrong results that look plausible. Being the kind of person who looks at a surprisingly good result and thinks "what did I break?" is incredibly valuable. Sanity checks, baselines, looking at the actual data rather than just the summary statistic. That instinct saves enormous amounts of time.

**Fluency with the tools.** PyTorch, tensor manipulation, being comfortable poking at a model's internals. If every operation is a struggle, you'll run fewer experiments and your intuitions will develop more slowly.

**Infrastructure and scale, at the frontier specifically.** Distributed training, managing compute efficiently, working with huge codebases, making things not fall over when you run them on thousands of chips. Labs are often bottlenecked on people who can make the machinery work. It's less glamorous than coming up with the clever research idea, but it's often the binding constraint.

**Taste about what to build.** Knowing when a quick hacky script is the right call and when it's worth investing in proper tooling that the whole team will use. Good engineers multiply the productivity of everyone around them.

The encouraging thing is that most of this is very learnable by just doing it. If you're a decent programmer, pick a small research project, replicate a paper, get your hands dirty. You'll learn far more from that than from reading about it. And honestly, I think a lot of people underrate how much safety work is engineering-bottlenecked. You don't need to be a research genius to make a big difference. Being someone who reliably gets things working is enormously valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a bunch of things here, and the honest answer is that it's a bit different from what people often expect. People sometimes imagine that what matters is being an incredibly elite software engineer in the sense of, like, you can write beautiful, well-architected production code. And that's valuable in some roles, but it's not actually the core thing for most research-adjacent work.

The skill I'd put at the top is what I'd call research engineering, or just being really fast and effective at building the thing you need to answer a question. Most of the work in a research team looks like: you have a hypothesis, you need to run an experiment to test it, and the bottleneck is how quickly you can go from idea to a working experiment to a plot you can actually learn from. So the valuable skills are things like being very fluent with PyTorch or JAX, being comfortable manipulating tensors and understanding what shapes things are and where the bugs are hiding, being able to write code that's good enough rather than perfect, and crucially being good at debugging. A huge fraction of research time is just things not working for mysterious reasons, and the people who are good at systematically narrowing down what's going wrong are enormously more productive.

Then there's a cluster of skills around infrastructure and scale. At a frontier lab, a lot of things that are trivial on a laptop become hard when you're dealing with very large models. So understanding distributed systems, how to shard a model across many accelerators, how to make data pipelines not be the bottleneck, how to profile and figure out why something's slow — people who are genuinely good at this are rare and extremely valued. It's not glamorous but it's load-bearing for everything.

And I'd also emphasise the meta-skills. Being able to notice when you're going down a rabbit hole and should step back. Having good taste about which experiments are actually informative. Writing clear enough code and notes that your collaborators, or you in three weeks, can understand what you did. Communication is weirdly underrated — a lot of the value of an experiment is lost if you can't explain what you found.

If I were giving advice to someone who wants to build these skills, I'd say: don't just do courses. Pick a small model, try to replicate a paper or do some little investigation, and push through all the annoying bits until you get a result. That process of fighting with real code on a real problem teaches you far more than anything else, and it's also the most convincing thing you can show a hiring manager.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between research engineering and the engineering that makes a large organisation’s infrastructure work reliably. Both are valuable, but they’re somewhat different skill sets.

For research engineering, I think a particularly valuable skill is being able to take a vague research idea and quickly turn it into an experiment you can trust. That means writing code, understanding what the experiment is actually testing, and being good at debugging when the results look weird. Is this an interesting scientific result, or did you accidentally mask out the wrong tokens? Being able to tell the difference is quite important.

There’s also a lot of value in understanding how to make models run efficiently: GPU programming, distributed systems, performance profiling, that sort of thing. If you can make a common experiment substantially faster, you’re potentially speeding up the work of a whole team.

And I wouldn’t underestimate fairly ordinary software engineering skills. Building something that other people can understand and use, choosing sensible abstractions, knowing when to write tests and when you’re overengineering a throwaway experiment. Research code has this awkward property where something you wrote for one afternoon can become the foundation of the next six months of work.

The common thread is being able to make progress under uncertainty. You often won’t get a beautifully specified task. You need to work out what matters, build something useful, and notice when it isn’t doing what you thought it was doing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most valuable thing is being able to take a fairly vague research idea and turn it into an experiment you can actually trust. That involves writing code quickly, but it also involves debugging, understanding what the results mean, and noticing when you’ve accidentally measured something different from what you intended.

A lot of people hear “engineering at a frontier lab” and think about incredibly specialised distributed systems work. And that is really valuable: if you can make training runs faster or more reliable, you can have a lot of impact. But there’s also a huge amount of value in being a strong generalist who can pick up an unfamiliar codebase, figure out what matters, and get something working without needing everything specified in advance.

I’d particularly emphasise having good feedback loops. Can you write a small test, look at the actual outputs, and catch a mistake before spending a week running experiments? Can you distinguish a real result from a bug? In research, code running successfully is a much weaker condition than the experiment actually answering your question.

So I’d worry less about knowing every fashionable framework and more about becoming someone who can reliably make progress on messy, unfamiliar problems.
